blocks.content: Two flags decide how a container occupies your terminal: -d runs it silently in the background, -it attaches your terminal directly to it. Picking the right one matters for whether your shell gets its control back immediately or not.
1. Detached Mode: Run and Walk Away
blocks.text: 1. Detached Mode: Run and Walk Away

blocks.content: With -d, Docker starts the container and immediately returns control of your terminal, printing just the new container's ID. The container keeps running in the background regardless of what your terminal does next.

blocks.alt: Your terminal is free again immediately

blocks.content:
docker run -d nginx
# a1b2c3d4e5f6...
# Your shell prompt returns right away, nginx keeps running.

code.content:
docker run -d nginx
# a1b2c3d4e5f6...
# Your shell prompt returns right away, nginx keeps running.

codes.bash:
docker run -d nginx
# a1b2c3d4e5f6...
# Your shell prompt returns right away, nginx keeps running.

blocks.content: 2. Interactive Mode: Your Terminal Becomes Its Terminal
blocks.text: 2. Interactive Mode: Your Terminal Becomes Its Terminal

blocks.content: -it (almost always used together: -i keeps stdin open, -t allocates a pseudo-terminal) attaches your actual terminal session to the container's process. Your shell is now occupied by that container until it exits or you detach.

blocks.alt: Your terminal is now the container's terminal

blocks.content:
docker run -it ubuntu bash
# Drops you straight into a bash prompt inside the
# container, your terminal is now attached to it.

code.content:
docker run -it ubuntu bash
# Drops you straight into a bash prompt inside the
# container, your terminal is now attached to it.

codes.bash:
docker run -it ubuntu bash
# Drops you straight into a bash prompt inside the
# container, your terminal is now attached to it.

blocks.content: The choice usually maps directly to what the container is for: a long-running service (a web server, a database) almost always runs detached, so it keeps running independent of your terminal session. A one-off debugging or exploration session almost always wants to be interactive, so you can actually see and type into it.

blocks.alt: Long-running services detached, debugging sessions interactive

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: -d runs a container in the background and returns your terminal immediately, the right default for long-running services.
-it attaches your terminal directly to the container, the right choice when you actually need to see and interact with it live.
